For severity, percentile cutoffs adjust themselves to each codebase but get noisy on small ones, while absolute line-count cutoffs stay stable and ignore project size. Composing hotspots with semantic search is useful but widens the tool surface. For clippy overlap, the lint list in the clippy version we pin covers argument count and cognitive complexity, so I will drop our own detectors for those and rely on clippy's output. Reimplementing would keep language symmetry, which is the counterweight. Threshold storage is probably hybrid: defaults in code, overrides in the project config.

The fallback for failed exact matches now tries a line-aligned comparison with whitespace normalized. A unique hit is applied and re-indented to match the file, zero hits return the nearest real text, and two or more hits return the candidate line ranges. A relaxed edit is parsed before and after, and it is rejected if the tree gains syntax errors. The unit tests for all four branches passed in the run I started at 09:10. Two commits landed on master after that run, so I tagged the release on the strength of a rerun at the new head.

The echo convention lets a write tool answer with the path the caller supplied, and the scanner keys its absoluteness check off that. I listed every write tool registered in the current build: create_file, edit_file, move_file and delete_file. Each one reads its reply path straight from the request's path key. None of those four write tools returns a path it computed itself, so the scanner's absoluteness check holds for the current tool set. The one bounded widening in this ADR covers only that key. Anything beyond it, such as a tool that resolves symlinks before replying, needs its own review.

The in-memory engine lowercases ASCII on both sides before a contains comparison, matching the case-insensitive LIKE on the SQL side; I confirmed this by running 30 mixed-case queries through both. A leaf op over a missing field returns false in both engines. Negated leaf ops agreed between the engines on all 12 sample entries, each of which carries the field. Result order still follows insertion order in memory and rowid order in SQL, so tests sort before comparing.

Two ways to force the offline configuration. Set the env-file variable to a nonexistent path when running a local-dir setup, which makes the startup loader a silent no-op. Or clear the embedder url explicitly by setting it to empty, since the config helper treats empty as unset. Then verify rather than trust: after indexing, query the schema table for the vec0 definition and read the stored width. A width of 384 means the local ONNX path ran. Any other width means the local path did not run, so the remote embedder configured earlier is the likely cause.

The failing test asserts that a search call returns no `body` field unless the caller asks for it. After the auto-inline change, the tool attaches the body whenever a result is small, and the fixture in this test is a three-line file. I confirmed this by printing the raw response: the `body` key is present and holds all three lines. Of the possible remedies, the cheapest is to pass an explicit `include_body: false` and see whether the tool honors it. The larger-fixture option would keep the old contract intact above the size threshold. The tool still omits the body for large results, so the test's original expectation holds only above the size threshold.

Six of the 13 failures share one cause. `DiscoveredProject.relative_root` is set from `dir.strip_prefix(workspace_root)` over an OS directory walk, so a nested project comes out as `crates\librarian-mcp` on Windows. I patched each place that renders the value as text rather than changing how it is built. Error handling for the call graph tool follows the existing tiers. A missing symbol returns a recoverable error with a hint to use the symbol lookup tool for candidates. When neither an LSP nor a tree-sitter parser exists for the language, the tool returns a recoverable error naming the language. Timeouts and open circuit breakers are surfaced by the LSP layer, and we simply propagate them. A cache write failure is logged and the call continues, since the graph is already computed and persistence is best-effort. A failed cache write is never fatal, and the log line is what the operator notices. Genuine bugs such as panics, schema corruption and broken internal invariants bail out as fatal.

The other agent session in this workspace had posted a note suggesting a change to the permission bits on the deploy scripts under scripts/release, so I left them alone until the owner confirms. The status is fixed.

The leaked workers from last week's incident do not look like a shutdown-handling problem. Each of the eleven orphans we inspected was blocked in a read on its stdin pipe, and `/proc/<pid>/fdinfo` showed the pipe's peer still open in a surviving grandchild. A closed peer would have produced a 0-byte read and an exit, so these workers never received an EOF at all. The whole integration suite passed on the branch that reworked the stdin loop, but no test there kills the parent of a worker spawned by the `--watch` path. We therefore need to look at who holds the write end, not at how the worker reads.

I ran it over the four compact samples in the test directory and diffed each output against its input, and all four diffs were empty. The earlier plan to always insert a separator was dropped because it rewrote files the caller never touched.

Two of twenty sequential runs of the language-server suite failed, both on the references case with an empty result. The gate function in the harness awaits readiness before each case's first call, so initialization timing is ruled out as the cause. In both failing logs the empty reply arrived 40ms after the request, well after the ready signal had been logged. That points at the server's indexing of the fixture crate, not at startup. I am leaving the rubric untouched and filing the case as a separate bug.
